item.title: an observation about dark ages
item.dc:creator: jenn
item.description:
our idea of what a "dark age" looks like seems hopelessly marred by survivorship bias. many civilizations/subcultures/genres of media don't exist anymore, and presumably it would be fair to characterize the period right before they wink out of existence as a dark age.

but the only dark ages that make it into the literature — medieval Europe, the slow attrition of LessWrong 1.0, the crash of comics as as a medium in the mid 90s — are the ones preceding something like a golden age. or at least a silver one.

i'm not sure what the base rates are, or how to distinguish between reference classes. we don't hear much from groups that don't exist anymore.

item.title: Market-Clearing Enthusiasm
item.dc:creator: jenn
item.description:
By the way, I run a semi-secret annual festival for Canadian rationalists. I try to keep the cost of attendance down, and I don't advertise it much outside of the group chats of the established meetup groups in the area (Waterloo, Toronto, Ottawa, Montreal). To even know where the ticket page is, you will need to be reasonably plugged into the IRL Canadian rat scene.1

To me, each year's festival feels a little like a cozy extended family reunion: every so often, a regular of one city will move to another, and it's a good opportunity for them to catch up with old friends and introduce them to new ones. We also have at least a few ex-regulars fly in from the Bay each year.

Well-meaning, economically minded friends tell me to charge more for tickets, and to advertise it more broadly. But I think this will make the festival worse.

Willingness to pay is a useful measure when you don't have higher quality ones available. But, like, I know a bunch of the Canadian rationalists. I was a regular for a bit in Ottawa, ran meetups in Waterloo, and now live in Toronto. And I keep bumping into Montreal rats on the broader festival circuit.

I know which people would be actively excited to come hang out, and which ones will be less enthusiastic about the venture. And some in the former group have basically no money, while some in the latter group have lots to spare. I would much rather gate attendance based on excitement and pre-existing commitment to the scene, and am lucky in that I am information-rich enough to be capable of doing so.

Another recurring festival that happens in my neck of the woods is Dashcon 2 — the recently revived unofficial tumblr convention. The organizers of the tumblr convention, appropriately, are disinclined to believe in market-clearing prices and have done as much as possible to make their ticket pricing accessible (i.e. cheap as hell), despite outsized demand for their product. The end result for both years they've run so far is that they crash the ticketing platform they use and sell out of tickets in ten minutes flat.

In an important way, this has worked out wonderfully in their favour: I've never seen a more enthusiastic, energetic, elaborately-cosplayed set of con attendees. This happens because they are limiting their tickets to only the most eager of their potential attendees — those who are willing to set a phone alarm to open up their ticketing website on a plethora of devices with their payment info ready to go, and panickedly hustle through filling out the payment form in the early hours of the day. But they are also selecting for attendees with the most slack and resources in their lives, and perhaps there are other things the organizers would rather select for.

When there is outsized demand for a thing, consider that it's sort of like having a budget of pretty extensible ways that you can use to whittle down who you want your customers/participants to be. You can set a market-clearing monetary price if you like, but sometimes you are lucky enough to have other options available. Can you select for enthusiasm? Talent? Duration in the community?

If you don't do this selection actively, sometimes it will happen for you anyways.

After moving from a city of almost 700,000 to a city of more than seven million, the attendance of my weekly meetups has increased only modestly. This was surprising to me at first, but now I have a good story for why this might have been the case: I require people to do readings and come to the meetups ready to discuss them, and the opportunity cost of homework is greater in a big city than it is in a college town. The enthusiasm that's required to attend is higher, such that a smaller percentage of potential attendees clear the market.

Eliot, who runs meetups in Australia, likes to describe his philosophy in the following way: "I believe in having wide open doors that are out of the way. That way people are already selected for door finding." I really like this.

Incidentally, a similar dynamic is why I like mostly writing here, on a blog that is out of the spotlight. I want the people who read me to have been pre-selected for.





  1. If you are Canadian and interested in attending, but you don't live in a city with an extant meetup group, message me and I'll see what I can do.↩

item.title: Easing Off The Gas
item.dc:creator: jenn
item.description:
Today is day ten of Inkhaven, and this is my tenth substantive post in as many days.

It was easy to publish every day as a member of the first Inkhaven cohort last November. I came to Berkeley with a list of blog post ideas, many fun and quick to write, and I was content to publish stuff that was mediocre on half the days. My job at the time was flexible and fairly chill too, and it was not too difficult for me to reduce my hours for the month.

I don't really identify as a writer, or, if I do, it comes second to my identity as a community organizer. It was difficult for me to agree to return to Inkhaven (having been invited to become an advisor), because it's hard for me to be away from my city and my meetups for long. I miss them, and I feel an acute dereliction of duty, and I feel guilt that I am neglecting the most important thing.

The only way that it could be okay, I thought, was if I fully took advantage of the month. If I did the challenge again, and wrung out all the words that had accumulated inside me. And so I began the challenge at the same time as the third cohort.

This time around, however, a few things are different.

My day job has greater demands of me. Not only do I have a direct report now, much is happening in the policy area that we are focused on, and there is a greater opportunity cost in not getting out the one-pagers and research analyses and proposed bill wordings expeditiously.

I am an advisor, which means I need to dedicate many hours each week to reading the work of the cohort, giving feedback, and designing and running writing-related programming.

As an advisor, I feel immense pressure to only publish works that are good, and not any works that are mediocre. I want to prove that I am a better writer than the residents, so that it makes sense for them to use me as a resource, instead of me being just a weird alum with extra privileges hanging around.

Ben had also made it clear to me how much he would appreciate my full commitment to writing during the month, so that we can help each other grow stronger as writers, and it could be a meaningful experience for us to share as a couple. The NRE is still pretty strong here, such that I really didn't like the idea of disappointing him.

Lastly, I have more drafts that I think are important for me to write with care (rather more care than I think is realistic for a daily publishing program), and not a lot of blog ideas that I think are "easy". Even the "easy" posts — such as Dressing for the Weather, or the Patrick Collison Takedown Post, ended up taking up more time than I thought. I somehow thought that I could knock out the takedown post in three hours, and it ended up taking me the greater part of two days. I had to clean up a draft I would have appreciated more time to consider the implications of and hurriedly publish it in the last few hours of Wednesday night, and this also left me almost no hours for doing my actual job.

I endorse all of these pressures. Still, this has had the unfortunate consequence of me not loving the writing process as much as it deserves to and should be loved. I want to write insofar as it nurtures my writing in all ways — not just the skill of it, but that it makes me feel positively towards the act of writing, and that it resolves dangling questions I have and makes me less confused about the world.

I have decided, therefore, to go on a publishing hiatus for the next ten days, and resume daily publishing for the final third of Inkhaven.

What will I do during my hiatus?

I will still be writing a lot, because there is much I want to write about this month. But without a daily deadline, I will be able to take greater risks in my writing, and cutting.

I will attend many more of the events that are put on by people in this cohort, and get to know the people in it better. I will visit friends in the area, and make new ones. I will make art — more stickers, and I'd like to do a Big Art Project with the cohort too, which might require figuring out the laser printer. I will spend a lot of time with Ben.

And maybe I will still publish a piece or two, if it makes sense to. But if not, I will see you on December 1st.

item.title: Patrick Collison you are WRONG about street furniture!!!
item.dc:creator: jenn
item.description:
I would like our public spaces to be more beautiful and comfortable. So would some other guys on the internet, but to me they seem pretty confused about the root cause of why they're ugly now.

Patrick Collison, for example, ponders:

Many things today are ugly and far uglier than they used to be or need to be. Once you see this, it’s kinda hard to stop perceiving it. (Early twentieth century phone boxes versus modern phone boxes; old water fountains versus new water fountains; etc.) As someone with a naively meliorist assumption that most things should be getting better rather than worse, it’s all a bit perplexing: why did we stop doing things nicely? Is it a choice? Was there a malevolent spell cast upon us?

At the end of his x post on this subject he appears to imply that this ugliness might be a marker of modern western culture's underlying metaphysical incoherence?

The illustrative example he provides is of two telephone booths, one strikingly red and beautiful and one black and utilitarian.

This is not a level 1 discourse topic. I know this because sometimes I am linked articles that are titled things like "Eight architecture myths BUSTED by Samuel Hughes" (a piece written, perhaps confusingly, by Ben Southwood), where you can infer from the title a whole universe of discourse where there are narratives and counter-narratives about modern architecture.

People who discoursepoast about this topic seem to really insist on the fact that there is in fact such a thing as spaces that are more objectively beautiful and humane, which, yes agreed, but they seem to think that the reason that things are ugly now is because there's some sort of... evil elite degeneracy or counter-signalling? Okay, um, straight off the bat here are some problems I notice with this hypothesis:

  • If you go to places where only the evil elites gather, such as Michelin star fine dining restaurants, too-fancy hotel bars like the one where I paid $47 US dollars 😔 for a whiskey sour, Google offices, Four Seasons resorts, or a certain compound in Berkeley, you will notice that their insides are more beautiful and comfortable for humans than the outside world tends to be.
  • As someone who went to school for urban planning, I do not remember being taught to design any public space in ugly or anti-human ways. In fact I strongly suspect that I attended hundreds of hours of lectures on and had my coursework graded on how to competently do the opposite.
  • Also, as someone who went to school for urban planning, the people who end up as urban planners are not, uh, particularly elite in any sense of the word.
  • Patrick Collison is a billionaire, and the "architecture myths BUSTED" piece is a part of the Stripe Press extended universe, i.e. Collison's propaganda unit, so it kind of appears to me like the anti-elite critique is coming from inside the house? Like, that's fine by me, the only way to defend against a bad billionaire with a gun is a good billionaire with a gun, that's what I always say (where ummmmm the guns are a metaphor for urban design preferences), it's just slightly inconvenient for this point, yeah?

Maybe the issue is that I am not sufficiently confused, but to me the problem seems to straightforwardly boil down to Baumol's cost disease. That is: some kinds of work get more productive per worker over time as we make technological breakthroughs (making cars, growing wheat) and some don’t (taking care of toddlers, playing in a string quartet). Wages rise in the first kind because each worker produces more, but this also creates significant pressure for wages in the second category of work to grow ~commensurately for ~reasons. Thus things like daycare and concert tickets explode in price, even if you're getting basically the same experience that your dad got for $20 thirty years ago.

As I said, this is not a level 1 discourse topic, which means that people have already taken a stab at objecting to this objection. For example, Southwood's piece says:

Myth two: buildings from the past are more beautiful, but only because they have more ornament, which due to the Baumol Effect, we can no longer afford. This theory is intuitive to a certain kind of economically minded person. This sort of person is less given to blindly trusting the cultural elites that the evidence their eyes give them is wrong, and notices that one of the main distinctions between postwar and prewar architecture is ornament, but expects that there must be a good reason for this. The proposed good reason is that ornament is intrinsically labor intensive, meaning that it gets more expensive when labor goes up in price due to technological progress.

...

The problem is that ornament doesn’t have to be labor intensive: it was already being industrialized in the time of the Romans! In fact, sculpture was not always by the named artist’s hand: it was usually done by an apprentice with a machine after a clay or plaster design by the master. By the late-nineteenth century, ornament was built at scale in factories, and the gigantic income and wage increases of the nineteenth century led to people consuming more and more of it. The Baumol story is not remotely tenable. [emphasis mine]

To summarize: we have the technology to mass-produce ornament, so it shouldn't be subject to the Baumol Effect. He also links to a piece titled The Beauty of Concrete, which makes the same argument: over time, less labor was necessary per unit of ornament, so ornament should not be subject to this effect, so the reason that things are ugly now must be because...

Because, um...

??????

If you are confident that it's not the Baumol effect, then the malevolent spell does seem at least as plausible as any other explanation. Fortunately, this so-called counter-argument is actually NOTHING, so gentlemen, please, we really don't need to start accusing each other of witchcraft!!!

A long time ago, I was on the steering committee of my university's initiative to add signage to our at-the-time almost entirely unlabelled campus. We worked with a competent regional urban design studio which came to us with many beautiful, elaborate, mathematically-inspired designs for wayfinding and building signage. We would excitedly socialize them to the internal team, then get repeatedly bitch slapped by the plant ops representative.

Plant Operations, for reference, is the support department "responsible for the maintenance, repairs, renovations and improvements of approximately 8,000,000 square feet of space across 70 buildings located on 1,112 acres of land."

Here is the sort of feedback that plant ops would give:

  • That dangly bit is going to get broken off and stolen by some drunken undergrad by homecoming weekend. How much would each replacement cost and how many do you want us to keep on hand?
  • You're thinking of using plastic? That's going to warp when we blast it with our power washer.
  • No, we can't use a more delicate cleaning mechanism, that'll slow us down too much. You're planning on having one per building entrance and a bunch on the pathways, they'll get vandalized at the rate of maybe three a week. The annual budget gets us fifty folks on grounds maintenance, and they're already overwhelmed with work as it is. Do you have additional ongoing budget for us?
  • No? Yeah, in that case, no plastic, no wood, no paint. I literally cannot emphasize to you enough how much you need this design to be able to withstand the power washer.

Plant ops feedback led our emails to look increasingly less and less ambitious in terms of design, and more and more like, well:

I can assure you, no one was happy about writing or receiving emails like this. We all loved the campus, and we wanted our addition to it to be beautiful. But our aspiration towards beauty was no match for the crushing, brutal logic of plant ops's annual personnel budget.

In the end, the signage that got rolled out was almost exactly what you'd expect from such a set of requirements.

(Actually, they got worse from this slide; after some more back and forths the translucent glass panel at the bottom was also replaced with plain black powder coated steel, leaving only the one at the top.)

So in short, though we had a very generous budget for designing and manufacturing the signage, all of our ambitions were blocked by the fact that there were only so many guys doing the groundskeeping. So like, I think this Baumol guy is maybe onto something.

Here’s another reason I think Baumol is right. Last fall I spent a weekend in Newport, Rhode Island, where the gilded age coal and rail magnates of New York built their summer mcmansions. At the time I was insanely locked in on some vampire fanfiction I was writing, and my vampiress OC dwelled and terrorized men in a mansion I’d heavily modeled after The Elms. I visited because I wanted a felt sense of how big the ballroom was and what the servants' quarters were like.

The grand entryway of The Elms. My beautiful vampiress Mary Sue blorbo was quite avant garde in her preference for sunlight and pale decor.

These days, the majority of the mansions are owned by the Newport Preservation Society. The preservation society is a nonprofit that turns them into museums that you pay money to enter, because that is the only way that they can pay for all the maintenance they need. Some of them were sold to the preservation society because the family trusts were fumbled in the century since their construction, but some belonged to families that still have significant means today. For example, it costs $32 USD to tour The Breakers, which once belonged to the Vanderbilt family.

The entry hall of The Breakers. The chandeliers can be gas-powered (hence the thick black rods), because the mansion was built before we invented reliable electrical grids.

If you looked up in any of the rooms it would kind of look like this. After visiting Newport I finally understood on a spiritual very fundamentally material level why it was called the "gilded age".

I suspect that gilded age mansions are the kind of thing that Patrick Collison wants more of; rooms and rooms of imported marble and beautiful intricate mosaic work and classy European portraiture.

The Vanderbilts (the Vanderbilts!!) could not keep up the army of fifty servants and twenty gardeners that was required to keep The Breakers running. Alice Vanderbilt’s death in 1934 passed the house to her youngest daughter Gladys, and even then it was common knowledge that the house was more of a liability than a gift. Gladys rented it out to the Preservation Society for $1 a year, and lived in a small apartment on the upper floor of the mansion while the rest of it was converted into a tourist attraction.

In 1972 Gladys' heirs sold it outright to the Society for $365,000 (what might be a sweetheart price, to be fair), at which point the annual spend was around $500,000 on wages, maintenance, and upkeep. The mansion was sold for less than the cost of a year of its own maintenance.

Contra the Works In Progress guys, I just, like, don't think the manufacture of the ornaments is the crux for whether or not the Baumol effect is to blame for why everything is bad now? I suspect what made the Vanderbilt heirs balk was the ongoing operational cost of hiring seventy people to maintain all that state-of-the-art stamped/cast/extruded gilt and the sophisticated garden grounds, not a newly trending preference for vandalism-proof plexiglass.

Let's now return to those two phone booths, and let me tell you what I would see as a municipal bureaucrat, a job that I am qualified to do and would have done in a very depressing alternate life.

First, I would recognize that the first phone booth, the painted red one, is beautiful. Of course it is. I vastly prefer it aesthetically over the plain utilitarian powder coated black steel and plexiglass.

But here are some other things that I would note:

  • The little raised crown at the top and the TELEPHONE label is going to trap grime and dust.
  • And each little corner of each little glass panel, because of the way the pane dividers stick out. You can already see the grime on the lower panels. The red paint will also make dirt unusually noticeable, which means it will need to be wiped down regularly.
  • The booth might also require regular repainting, especially if we are wearing down the red paint by exposing it to cleaning agents regularly. Because of all the little glass panels that we don't want to get red paint over, the repainting will be finicky and arduous.
  • If the door is accidentally left open, or blown open by the wind, leaves and detritus will get inside, so someone will need to go in and clean the floor inside on a regular basis.
  • Some animal might make a nest inside, or get trapped and die inside and then it will be unusable until we call animal control (expensive).
  • It will be peed in, slept in, and used for drugs. No one can see in properly, which might make it unsafe.
  • Will the door freeze shut in January? Can a snowplow get near it, or will someone need to shovel out a path to the door manually? Or do we only use them half the year?
  • Is it wheelchair accessible?
  • How many additional full-time unionized public service workers do we need to hire to take care of every, say, fifty of the red phone boxes? Can we justify raising property taxes to hire people for this?

It brings me no pleasure to observe that the fuck-ugly metal box solves all these problems, and every attempt to engineer the red box to solve the above problems will make it more like the ugly one.

Things are ugly because the street sweepers are basically doing the same thing that they were doing a hundred years ago. But these days instead of hiring, I dunno, wretched street orphans for a pittance (as a civilization we made the choice to eliminate "wretched street orphan" as a category of worker), we have to pay grown adults full municipal union wages and benefits.

Okay, fine, so are we cursed to have bad street furniture forever? Do we have to be resigned to this?

I mean, personally, I think we just need to let the industrial designers cook, and come up with nicer designs that meet the requirements.

The new requirements are pretty well specified, and you can find them in documents such as Vibrant Streets, Toronto's Street Furniture Design and Policy Guidelines (section 6.5):

  • Materials and finishes must have proven their long term ability to function in and withstand severe environmental conditions (i.e. snow, ice, salt, pollution etc.), while maintaining their appearance.
  • Materials must have proven success in terms of their intended use and ability to withstand vandalism and other abuse.
  • Elements must be fabricated to the highest standards and have a proven track record of use in high traffic environments.
  • Repair must be easy. Replaceable modular parts should be designed to make repair easy, so that elements are not “out of service” for any length of time.

I think these are pretty reasonable guidelines for street furniture design considering Baumol's constraints, though there is of course room to quibble on the margin. But I think ultimately my intuition is that, like — how many man-hours do you think have gone into the creation of street furniture that is beautiful, and can also adhere to these guidelines? Like, probably we just haven't poured enough effort into the problem yet? I feel content to just chill and wait.

Also, can I say something a bit out of pocket? Okay, okay, look. It appears to me..... that we are not exactly sending our best into the field of industrial design. And I find this to be a very reasonable allocation of talents, because probably we want to allocate our best to, like, solving cancer or AI misalignment, and not the marginal improvement of park benches?

Our brave b-tier troops are trying their best to design beautiful street furniture in accordance with the new requirements imposed by the rising cost of human labour. It's probably okay if they need a little extra time; nothing's going to explode.

I am content to chill and wait, because what I notice is that over time the public spaces I am in have gotten incrementally more beautiful. When I go to Toronto's newest park, I find the street furniture there to be more pleasing than the generic street furniture I remember growing up with.

Some intriguing seating(?) by the giant owl.

A covered, strawberry-themed rest area.

I'll be the first to admit that it's not at gilded age levels of impressiveness yet. If one is more impatient than me, and would desire things to improve faster, I hear funding for more R&D helps. Either for more beautiful benches, or for automated robot labour. Does anyone have Collison's number?

item.title: Notes on Differentiated Social Awareness
item.dc:creator: jenn
item.description:
You don't need to tell your fat friend that they should consider losing weight, or that they should get on a GLP-1. Your fat friend already knows.

You might not need to tell your female friend who has disordered eating practices that they have an eating disorder. Your female friend has probably been in a middle school health class about how a significant fraction of girls will struggle with disordered eating in their lifetime. Your female friend has likely experienced many discourse cycles about disordered eating practices. But it's also very possible she's somehow convinced herself that her own case doesn't count for whatever reason. Or perhaps she's the kind of person who never took any of the PSAs seriously, and thinks that almond moms are behaving in perfectly acceptable ways.

You probably need to tell your male friend who is working out and cutting a lot that he might have an eating disorder. Disordered eating is not yet a concept that we have made readily available to men, despite men making up something like one quarter to one third of people with eating disorders.

The above set of claims has the following potential weaknesses:

  • Many people these days seem to have like only one to three friends, such that there isn't much of an information environment to model.
  • Many people find it very difficult to say true things when it is sufficiently awkward for them, such that obvious balls get dropped all of the time.

There is much additional throat clearing one can do about the above claims but I trust the reader to be able to generate them or to ask their preferred LLM for a list. I shall move on to my actual point.

In general, if you want to help someone who is dealing with some kind of difficult ongoing problem, it can be useful to develop a model of the information environment that your friend is living in.

The core move I want to articulate is to think about what the default, intuitive social response is1, and if you assess it to be oversupplied or otherwise unhelpful, to situate yourself somewhere a little less intuitive.

Sometimes the default, intuitive social response is good. If someone is going through a bad breakup, they will probably want a lot of support, as much as possible, so you might as well take them out for brunch and be another set of sympathetic ears as they pour out their woes to you.

Sometimes, the default, intuitive social response is good but only in limited quantities, and the general information environment way oversupplies it. It's probably good for your depressed, unemployed friend to know that it's likely beneficial for them to go back to school or to try to get a job or at least go to the gym. But the thing that they would find really helpful is not one more person telling them that or exhorting them to do so.

Sometimes the default, intuitive social response is actively bad and counterproductive. I write in detail about one case of this, when a friend is in an abusive relationship.

Often, what makes a social response the default, intuitive one is that it is a pareto optimal move that does not require much effort or risk on the part of the person performing it. This means that in situating yourself somewhere else often requires doing more work, or feeling more uncomfortable. You can offer to be gym buddies with your depressed friend, but this might incur more of a cost for you — for example, you will then need to then go to the gym yourself 😔.

Some of the most sophisticated social moves I have heard of require active strategizing and cooperation. For example, I know of one man who is the topic of a group chat he is not in. The group chat is for all of his friends and caretakers who are supporting him through his deep depression. It's a utilitarian, functional place, where people post sign-offs when they need to leave for work or sleep, and another person or two will offer to tag themselves in and note how long they'd be available for. I heard about this group chat at a brunch, and I don't know most of the people involved. I wonder how much intuition and how much strategy was required to build this chat.





  1. If you don't have a good sense of what the default, intuitive social response is, uh,,,, I don't really know if this is going to be a particularly useful post for you.↩

item.title: Canadian Woman Discovers Dressing for the Weather
item.dc:creator: jenn
item.description:
At six, I knew more or less how to dress appropriately for the weather. At twenty-six, I could not.

At six, I knew the rules: when it is cold, wear sweaters. When there is a lot of snow on the ground, wear parkas and snow pants and snow boots. When it is hot, wear t-shirts and shorts. I was happy to go outside every recess and play on the playground, or the grass, or the snow, because I followed the rules.

At twenty-six I had more than a decade's experience of breaking the rules, and I was less delicate: I could tolerate being a little cold or a little hot without throwing a tantrum. Dressing appropriately for the weather frequently trades off against aesthetics, and I had grown to be quite an aesthete.

If you are an aesthete about your wardrobe, here is what happens. Your good winter coat goes out of style, or you lose it at a party, and you don't bother to buy a new one because the fall jackets you have drape better anyways, so why not just suck it up and wear those. You wear through your old boots and get new ones almost purely for how cool they look, rather than evaluating them on their ability to keep you warm and dry through the Canadian winter.

At some point, I stopped seeing clothing as technology, and started seeing it as decoration. I have a summer wardrobe, thin fabrics that I can layer, and a winter wardrobe where I play with knits and wools and fur, and twice a year I switch out what's in the storage tub and what's in my closet. If you live in a city, you don't really need to think about it more than that.

Then, I was tricked by some friends into going winter camping in the Yukon.

Up in the far north, even in the bright sun of midday, as soon as I got out of the heated car I began to freeze. My toes lost sensation halfway through the short walk despite my socks and lined boots, my thin wool gloves absorbed the cold, attracted little ice crystals, and began to suck the heat from my fingertips. The cold found its way through every little crevice of my bulky sweater and my down parka to trail its fingers up my belly and down my neck.

The walk from the car to the building where we were to be kitted up with our rented deepwinter gear took three minutes, and it would take thirty for the feeling to half-return to my toes.

A few pieces of the appropriate winter gear were brand new to me — the Sorel Glaciers, for example, with their huge chunky rubber bottom soles, a thick removable inner boot, a third layer of insole inside the inner boot; all those separate layers to insulate you from the ground that you walk upon.

But most of what we rented turned out to be stuff you can buy at any sporting goods store — polyester (😔) quarter zips and thermal leggings. It was given to us along with the layering advice I had been hearing and ignoring since time immemorial: wear multiple layers, tuck them into each other so the cold air can't get in, cover up your skin with hats and scarves. We layered larger parkas over smaller puffer coats, thick mittens over gloves over an inner thin glove, three layers of bottoms and then waterproof snowpants on top.

Thus dressed, I went outside again. And then, for the first time since I was small, I felt free. I could go inspect the parked sleds that we would be learning to use, go play with the dogs in their enclosures, amble to the treeline and look up at the generously snow-laden branches.

When you are not dressed for the weather, being outside imposes a small, continual cost. You want to get out of the rain, the cold, the beating sun. That was okay though, you assure yourself, because it was only for a little bit of time, and you would soon be comfortable inside again.

I made a little bargain in this shape over and over again, aesthetics over function, until it became second nature, and the understanding that I could be comfortable outside if only I was dressed for it turned as abstract as the knowledge that the earth was round and not flat.

In the frozen northern -35°C windchill, I felt freer outside than I ever did in southern Ontario. I had an abundance of time; I didn't have to plan out the most efficient path. How queer, how sweet, how luxurious.

Now I have a rack of coats suitable for every degree of cold and wet, and a small new collection of pretty wool scarves. Without the nudge of the Yukon trip, left to my own devices, I would have accumulated a rack of fall jackets and weird pants. Now I buy a greater panoply of things, careful to make sure that they are not only beautiful but fill functional holes in my wardrobe.

In shitty weather I used to walk to the bus stop grim-faced and hunched over. These days, I dress well, and leave ten minutes early so I can loop by my favourite neighbourhood cafe for a little treat. In July I enjoy the crash of rain, in January the crunch of snow. I want to keep ambling, and I often do.

item.title: partial parallels
item.dc:creator: jenn
item.description:
content warning: oops! all throatclearing :(

by the way, there are some blatant textual parallels between how to get a friend to leave an abusive relationship and on friends at frontier labs. a lot of my recent writing (on antimemes, and easier to be good) have been building up scaffolding and getting some loud tangents out of the way, so that i can write on friends at frontier labs and clarify my own thinking on the matter. all of those other pieces contain models that seem strongly but only partially instructive when i think about having friends at labs.

after several false starts in writing on friends at frontier labs, what got the words to flow was to put the draft side by side with my finished piece on abusive relationships, and to let myself self-plagiarize generously.

this unfortunately sort of leaves a shadowy rhetorical move where i am strongly implying that frontier labs are like abusive romantic partners, but i do not endorse this in any real way.

like, often things are like other things, but it's not that deep! for example, some similarities are:

  • people tend to spend time focusing on what is important to them
  • it is easier to get mad at people and yell at them when you want to get them to stop doing a thing, but it seems to me like often the more productive thing to do is to provide them lots of support, so that they have a little more slack
  • it's can be helpful to model people as being conflicted and confused under stressful environments, and then think "what kinds of support would I appreciate when I am conflicted and confused under stressful environments".

to put it another way, maybe there's like, what, a 30% similarity between these two things, but other things that can share a 30% similarity to an abusive relationship include

  • having a newborn
  • founding a startup
  • training for the olympics
  • caring for a parent with dementia
  • entirely healthy romantic relationships

such that i do not really endorse any amount of valence rub-off.

the obvious difference that the lab employees are not being negatively coerced to stay. the frontier labs are not holding any lab employees hostage, and the reason that they are staying is because they seem to truly believe that they are doing the right thing.

i think the strongest opinion i really have at this point is like, hey if you are trying to get lab employees to quit by getting mad at them (which i think is a framing that the deeprats don't endorse, but somehow this is the felt experience of everyone i know who is working at a lab) this seems counterproductive to your own goals.

i am aware that that take makes me "atheist telling the christians that they are practicing their religion wrong"-coded, but you know what sometimes that is what being a blogger is all about.

item.title: On Friends at Frontier Labs
item.dc:creator: jenn
item.description:
I am deeply uncertain about whether or not it is a good idea to get my friends to quit working at frontier AI labs. I am against people working at frontier AI labs in general, but perhaps downstream of this, all my friends in the labs have sophisticated justifications for their being there that seem plausibly true to me. More broadly, if this was not a painfully difficult question, the community wouldn't have split over it, and there are enough rationalists and EAs in the labs that it seems obvious to me that the community has split.

So I don't really get my friends to try to quit their jobs, as much as try to help them regularly orient to whether or not they should — and they generally humour me by treating this as a live question. I let them know frequently that I have reservations about their work, but also that I generally trust their judgement and care about them as people.

Here are my intuitions for what my friends are experiencing, while they are working at a frontier lab:

They value their job. Their job is giving them silly amounts of money and validation and prestige. Their job lets them work on a really important project with really smart people in comfortable settings. Their job gives them purpose. They believe that they are doing the right thing, and that they can more or less trust the leadership, or that even if they can't trust the leadership fully, every other player is less trustworthy.

They likely know that some people disagree with their choice to work at a frontier AI company and want them to feel shame about it. They actually know much more about the really cursed tradeoffs and clusterfucks that are happening inside their company than I do. But they will take pains to hide this ammunition from me, an outsider with reservations about their work — even if they haven't signed NDAs or have permissive ones, they will feel protective of the company, all the brilliant wonderful people that they know as colleagues, and their hopes for the work itself and the future that it might bring into being.

My friends are often scared, stressed, sleep-deprived, and in what I perceive to be an actively adversarial information environment. But I am also scared, stressed, and in an actively adversarial information environment (according to them). For my part I do try to prioritize good sleep hygiene.

There are people, including some that they look up to intellectually, who are in the process of repeatedly and loudly expressing disapproval at their choice to work at a frontier AI lab. Oliver Habryka and Eliezer Yudkowsky yells at respond disagreeably to their compatriots on X every time they choose to voice a pro-lab take. Ben Pace (disclosure: long Pace1) might be messaging them deranged stuff on Signal like "Good seeing you at the house party. By the way I think if we are living in a sane world you would be sentenced to ten thousand years in prison." High decouplers, man.

I think it's good that the deeprats (shhhh just go with it) do this. There should be some voices of general disapproval, and there is much value in saying socially aggressive and unpleasant true things. And they sure do have the right temperament for doing that job, unlike me.

The failure mode I see in this strategy is that they might make the lab employees tense and guarded and defensive around them, and nudge them that much further into an echo chamber comprised only of their sympathetic colleagues inside the frontier labs, all with their own well reasoned and sophisticated justifications for staying. Would it be too galaxy brained to claim that this might make them less likely to quit a harmful job?

For my part, as I know about the existence of the deeprats and their general MO, I think it is reasonable for me to try a different tack. The risk of this tack is that not only will I feel like an enabler, I might actually be an enabler. In this way, I might be making them less likely to quit a plausibly harmful job.

I mean, the deal is, I can't make people quit their job. And maybe it doesn't make sense for them to quit their job — like I said, I am deeply unsure. But I think my friends appreciate the ear of an unsettled third party, who has reservations about their work but is open to hearing them out about their beliefs. I think it's bad for people who are conflicted, as my friends tend to be, to only be able to talk to people who have already chosen sides. I think it makes it harder for them to figure out what they believe in, and whether or not their beliefs are true.

I have never gotten a friend to quit working at a frontier AI lab, though one of them quit of their own volition after one year, to resume their work on technical alignment.

It is fortunate that I am actually uncertain about whether or not it is reasonable for people who care about x-risk to work inside frontier labs, because I think it would be somewhat dishonest to pretend that you are uncertain for the purposes of "helping" your friend "orient". How convenient for me.





  1. ...also, I've smooched him approximately fifty times today.↩

item.title: Easier To Be Good
item.dc:creator: jenn
item.description:
I do not consider myself a good person. I am lazy and frivolous and inconsiderate, I care too much about intelligence and status, I am a snob and a hypocrite, and I do not call my mother enough.

I don't mean this to read as self-hatred, nor a show of false modesty. Among all the people I know there is only a scant handful of people I would consider genuinely good, and so it is unremarkable to me that I wouldn't find myself amongst their number.

You do not need to be good to desire more goodness in the world. It is good for everyone when things are good, and when there is more of it — more thoughtfulness, more generosity, more coordination, more care, more beauty, more clarity, more positive sum trades, more sophistication and elegance in our solutions and resolutions.

Increasing the amount of goodness in the world is an urgent project. The world really sucks right now, and even in the wealthiest enclaves of the imperial core there is an immense amount of suffering.

To reach the healed world would be a massive complicated undertaking. It is such a massive complicated undertaking that it is not enough for only those who are intrinsically good to work on it. There simply aren’t enough of them.

If it is desirable (as I contend) for morally mediocre people like me to work on the project, it would not be enough to appeal to their innate goodness, for they have not that much of it to be appealed to. You will need to offer me things that are more base, like status and money and the affirmation that I am a good person (for everyone wants to be a virtuous person and to be recognized as such, whether or not they are).

Fortuitously, there was an instructive breakthrough around a decade ago: effective altruism. Here's approximately what that is: you take people who come from the morally bankrupt culture that is the western professional managerial class, and you give us the prestige and status and affirmation of virtue we neurotically crave for the trivial cost of ten percent of our income and a few weekends a year where we are subject to vegan food and like sixteen hours of one-on-one discussions with a bunch of earnest dorks. As a result, suddenly a contingent of this culture begins to compete in a new arena of QALYs and utilons and eyestalk ablation literature reviews rather than the traditional arena of summer home square footage and the number of Michelin star restaurants one has set foot in.

Put it that way, and it doesn't sound so different from the beautiful promise of capitalism: that if we can successfully align the system with human values, it will result in some sort of elegant virtuous cycle such that people can go about selfishly pursuing their self-interested goals, and end up pouring immense amounts of goodness into the world as a side product.

As a mediocre person, it does sure seem self-evident to me that the only way to get mediocre people to do good, en masse, is to generate more selfish incentives for doing so. Whether capitalism has successfully done that is discoursebait I will leave to more foolhardy poasters.1 What I know for sure is that effective altruism did this for me. I dedicate much more of my energy and my money towards the reduction of suffering of sentient beings than I otherwise would, by a really really really wide margin.

It did this by not only appealing to some of my best instincts, but also some of my ugly ones, and ones that are simply mammalian. The community gave me peers that respected me and pushed me towards more virtuousness. I have recognition for my talents, and social status, and the occasional extra bag of money bit of funding when I do things that are unusually aligned with their goals. Insofar as engaging in effective altruism makes me do more improving things for the world than I would otherwise, it seems wise to continue to engage with it: to reap all of the rewards and allow myself to enjoy them to the fullest without guilt, such that I have as much motivation as I can get to continue to do good things for the world.

I am impure, so perhaps it is unsurprising that I've always disliked purity in my politics. Stringent, inhuman standards do not seem to me like the most effective way to increase the amount of goodness in the world. More specifically, stringent, inhuman standards will get you the small minority of humans who are inhumanly virtuous, and leave the rest of us out. To me that feels like leaving resources on the table.

I am not a good person, but I am a better one than I was before people started paying me in tangibles and intangibles to act like one. I would like as many people as possible to experience this privilege. For that to be the case, we will need to be thoughtful about how to bring more people into the fold — how to create a culture in which it is easier for people to be good.





  1. ...And my footnotes. I recognize that neither capitalism or the effective altruist ecosystem is as well aligned as its ideal versions would be, but this does not overly trouble me. Alignment problems of all kinds are wicked and difficult, and it makes sense to me that the very complicated ones (that won’t kill us imminently) might take up to centuries to straighten out. As long as there is continual improvement, I feel okay with the slowness of the bend towards justice.↩

item.title: Animal Husbandry Machines of Loving Grace
item.dc:creator: jenn
item.description:
Because I am an urbane cosmopolitan who was animal welfare pilled by the effective altruists rather than by firsthand experience interfacing with animals, I've been finding Wendell Berry's agrarian writings to be very illuminating. I often think of this idyllic scene in The Need to be Whole (2022):

An Amish family long dear to me bases the commercial part of its economy mainly on a dairy herd of forty-­five Jersey cows, for which the family’s small farm produces the necessary feed. From this modest enterprise the family achieves a “quality of life” that is admirable. They recently built themselves a new house. At the time of my last visit the farmwife and her two daughters, then seven and ten years old, were busy at the evening milking. It was a happy scene. The mother and daughters cooperated perfectly, each doing her share according to her strength. They kept steadily at work without haste or fuss. Each of the cows was known by her looks, character, and name. The family’s living was being made within a pattern of familiar relationships. The people and the cows knew, understood, and respected one another, which was why the barn stayed so noticeably quiet. The physical work, to which our society has cultivated an aversion, was done with skill, with care, without stress, without lasting too long or becoming in any way a hardship, and allowing for conversation with visiting friends. This twice-­a-­day chore was taking place where both the people and the animals were at home.

Until reading this, I had no real idea of the... depths? heights? of the ethical treatment of farm animals. The animal welfare EAs crunch the numbers and focus on the reduction of the cruelest practices that one might find in the factory farms, and I am deeply grateful for their important work.

It is not their fault that I somehow had no notion that the animals could be happy, and in relationships with humans, instead of just being marginally less miserable. But now I have this notion, and it is one that I find beautiful. It makes me happy to think about.

Berry goes on to point out that somewhere between fifty and a hundred cows, a farm operation will no longer be able to form familial relationships with the cows. At scales of over a hundred cows or people, it becomes functionally impossible to not treat them as identical, expendable, replaceable. These days, it is not uncommon to have 10,000 cow dairies, and the biggest ones in the world have over 100,000.

We are currently living in the middle of an intelligence explosion. A question that is useful to ask these days: what can we do if we are able to wield a billion times the intelligence that our civilization currently has?

Some animal welfare effective altruists are starting to think about this. Itsi Weinstock wrote The State of the AIxAnimals Field in April 2026, there was an AI x Animals week on the EA forum over the summer. This lit review highlights eight sub-themes of the fledgling movement:

  1. Getting the values we align AI to to include animal welfare
  2. Farm sensor and camera tech
  3. Anti-poaching and biodiversity monitoring
  4. AI models that could replace animal testing
  5. Decoding animal communication, like sperm whale codas
  6. Animal advocacy uplift
  7. AI-guided genetics for reducing animals’ capacity to suffer
  8. Longtermist wild animal suffering reduction

I am not surprised by the list! It's very EA, urbane cosmopolitan data spreadsheets coded. Probably it is a reasonably good list of what priorities we should have. But now I want it to be more ambitious, more wholesome.

If we do not get rid of animal husbandry as a practice, I hope some of our additional intelligence goes directly to the cows. Let our barns become as peaceful and quiet as those of the Amish. I hope each individual animal that depends on humans for survival has a little robot guardian angel who has the autonomy and resources necessary to care for it well, to get to know it as well as it deserves to be known, and knows exactly where it prefers to be scritched.
